title: Laughing and weeping
hook: Democritus laughed at the world, Heraclitus wept; Montaigne prefers laughter (Essays 1.50)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the back shop: a room all your own, behind the counter. Did you get your ten minutes, or did somebody knock? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

Two philosophers step out of their front doors and look at the same street. The same crowd, the same squabbles, the same people hurrying to things that won't matter by next year. One of them laughs. The other one cries. That's the whole story, and Montaigne didn't invent it; he found it in older writers. What he adds is a vote. Asked to pick a face for looking at the human race, himself included, he picks one, and his reason isn't about comfort.
screen: `ONE STREET, TWO PHILOSOPHERS.` → `ONE LAUGHS, ONE CRIES.` → `MONTAIGNE VOTES.`

segments.voice: First, the two faces. In his essay Of Democritus and Heraclitus, Montaigne says Democritus found the human condition vain and ridiculous, and never went out in public without a mocking, laughing face. Heraclitus, feeling pity for that same condition, went about with a sad face and eyes full of tears. Same world. Opposite weather. Second, the vote. Montaigne says he prefers the first: the laugh. But not, he says, because laughing is more pleasant than weeping. He prefers it because it's more disdainful. It condemns us more. It seems to him that we can't be looked down on as much as we deserve. That's sharper than a cheerful shrug. His laugh has an edge, and he points it at all of us, himself first. Third, the reason underneath. He says he doesn't think there's as much misery in us as there is vanity, or as much malice as foolishness. We're not so much wicked as silly. Not so much tragic as empty-headed. And that changes which face fits. Tears take our follies seriously, as if they were grand. A laugh cuts them back to their real size. Fourth, the gentle version. Montaigne's laughter can bite. Today's practice keeps the part that helps: laughing at self-importance, starting with our own. The email rewritten six times. The grudge over a parking spot. The fear of looking foolish, which is itself a little foolish. Seen from a step back, a lot of it is comedy.
screen: `ONE LAUGHED, ONE WEPT.` · `HE PREFERS THE LAUGH.` · `LESS MALICE THAN FOLLY.` · `LAUGH, STARTING WITH YOURSELF.` · then, large: `LAUGH, DON'T WEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at one thing gently. Sit, and let the breath slow down. Pick one thing of your own you've been taking very seriously. Not a real grief; something smaller. A worry about what someone thinks, a plan you've redone too many times, a little rivalry. Now look at it the way Democritus might, from a step higher up the street. A person, hurrying, very sure this matters. If a smile comes, let it. Keep it kind, and keep it pointed at yourself, not at anyone else. The bell holds the time.
Laughing and weeping. Democritus laughed at the human condition, Heraclitus wept, and Montaigne chose the laugh, because our trouble is less malice than folly. Today's word.
Your line: laugh, don't weep. Today, when you catch yourself being very important about something small, notice it, and let yourself smile. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as permission to meet human folly, their own first, with a laugh rather than despair, keeping cruelty out of it.

fork.setup: you look out at the human comedy, yourself included, and you have to choose a face. which does Montaigne choose?
options: keep a blank face and say nothing.
fork.reveal: he picks the laugh, and not for comfort: he says it's more disdainful, and we can never be looked down on as much as we deserve.

trapdoor: what you thought: Montaigne is telling us to look on the bright side.
what it means: laughter keeps our self-importance at its real size; tears treat our follies as if they were grand.
what a scholar hears: his laugh has an edge. he says it's more disdainful and condemns us more, and he puts himself inside the joke.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt

Numbering follows the outline (1.50, Villey); Cotton numbers it 1.50 as well in some editions, 1.49 in others; confirm.
